html:
The Benguela railway runs across Angola from the Atlantic port of Lobito to the border of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, about 1,300 km inland. It was built from 1903 to 1929 to carry copper from the mines of Katanga to the sea.

The line was built by a British company headed by Robert Williams, a partner of Cecil Rhodes, with a concession from Portugal. At the Congo border it joined the Katanga lines of the Union Minière, giving the copper belt a short route west to the Atlantic instead of the long haul to the Indian Ocean.

It also opened central Angola to Portuguese settlers and trade. During the Angolan Civil War after 1975 the line was cut and wrecked, and through traffic stopped for nearly thirty years. Chinese companies rebuilt it, and it reopened to the border in the 2010s. Today, as the Lobito Corridor, it is backed by the United States and Europe as an outlet for Congo's and Zambia's copper and cobalt.
